items.excerpt: スピッツがニューアルバム『kettle』を2026年11月25日（水）にリリースする。 スピッツの18作目のオリジナルアルバム『 kettle 』がついに完成し、発売が決定した。さらに、2027年3月から全国ツアー〈SPITZ JAMBOREE TOUR 2027 “kettle”〉が開催されることも決定した。 前作『 ひみつスタジオ 』（2023年）から3年半ぶりのアルバムとなる『kettle』には、8月7日の配信開始以降、Billboard JAPANの総合ソングチャート〈JAPAN Hot 100〉で5週連続トップ10入りを記録するなど好調なチャートアクションを続けているTBS系金曜ドラマ「Tシャツが乾くまで」の主題歌“ 見知らぬ糸 ”や、現在放映中のキリン午後の紅茶FRUITS & ICE TEA〈午後のフルーツティー〉篇のCMソング“キツネノボタン”、TVアニメ「SPY×FAMILY」Season 3のオープニング主題歌“ 灯を護る ”含む、全13曲が収録される。

items.body: Mala Fama‘s Río Cayápas and NXDLLI offer two complementary readings of the same journey. Both emerged from Esteban Farinango’s time in the Afro-Ecuadorian community of Telembí in Esmeraldas and were developed simultaneously, before OTONO label head Luis Clériga suggested presenting them as a double release. Río Cayápas stays close to communal music-making, while NXDLLI carries traces of these experiences into more abstract and introspective territory. Río Cayápas makes its intentions immediately clear. It opens with field recordings that place the listener in a specific environment before entering into what the liner notes describe as a dialogue with “local ethnic and autochthonous sounds.” Traditional rhythms from the province of Esmeraldas, recorded in the Telembí community, provide the foundation. Electronics work closely within this material, reinforcing percussion, marimba and voices until the boundaries between acoustic performance and electronic intervention become difficult to locate. NXDLLI turns towards resonance, atmosphere and slowly shifting textures, with rhythm largely receding from view. Recordings made in Esteban’s hometown of Ibarra filter quietly through the album, sometimes almost imperceptibly, particularly in “wakay”, “minervita” and “AMSA”. Environmental sounds become fragments of acoustic memory, retaining a connection to place even as their original context grows indistinct. Heard together, the two records continually illuminate one another. Río Cayápas foregrounds community, ritual and embodied rhythm; NXDLLI draws those experiences into introspective electroacoustic landscapes. Their shared sources make the differences between them all the more revealing. The accompanying remix collection demonstrates how much possibility remains within Mala Fama’s material. Each contributor finds something different in the originals. Entrañas draws out memory and dream; Omaar pushes the rhythms towards deconstructed bass; The Hissed finds unexpected harmonic warmth through ambient drum & bass; Viiaan turns birdsong into the principal melodic voice; Siete Catorce amplifies the ritual energy already embedded in the percussion; DNZA reveals surprising correspondences between Afro-Ecuadorian rhythms and footwork; and Quixosis dissolves the project into ambient resonance, bringing it close once again to landscape. Across both albums, traditional and electronic elements share the same musical space without settling into a clear hierarchy. Farinango allows percussion, marimba, voices, field recordings and electronics to interact until their respective roles become increasingly porous. Río Cayápas and NXDLLI trace the same journey through northern Ecuador from different perspectives, preserving the immediacy of encounters in Telembí alongside the altered forms those experiences assume through distance and memory. To trace the river back to its source, I caught up with Esteban over Zoom. NXDLLI and Río Cayápas explore the same path from two distinct perspectives. One is more closely linked to electroacoustic experimentation and ambient textures; the other foregrounds the music and rituals of Esmeraldas. At what point did you realize that this project needed to be divided into two releases? Was this an idea that was present from the beginning or did it emerge naturally during the creative process? My creative process isn’t linear. I never begin by thinking, I’m going to make an album. I’m always collecting sounds. Wherever I go, I record things that interest me because I’m constantly looking for material to experiment with. When I travelled to Esmeraldas and spent time in an Afro-Ecuadorian community, I recorded field recordings, instruments and all kinds of everyday sounds. From the beginning, I wanted to create something that captured the atmosphere of that place. A lot of projects combine electronic music with traditional music, but the two often remain separate—as if the electronics exist on one side and the traditional instruments on the other. I wanted to avoid that. My intention was to preserve the roots of the music while introducing just enough electronics to place it within a contemporary context. To me, that approach makes the music feel more alive. I love techno and electronic music, but sometimes purely electronic music can feel a little soulless. I wanted the electronics to support the traditional music rather than dominate it. At first, I was simply planning to make an EP. Around that time I received a grant from SAYCE—the Ecuadorian authors’ and composers’ society—which allowed me to develop the project properly. I initially wrote three tracks based on the material I had recorded in Esmeraldas. At the same time, though, I was recording completely different sounds closer to home. My grandmother would take me to waterfalls and perform prayers for my journey, surrounding me with flowers and blessings. I recorded her voice, the river, the birds—everything around us. Those recordings gradually led me towards another idea: creating long, ambient pieces built from atmosphere rather than rhythm. So I found myself working on two projects simultaneously. Then I met Luis Clériga from the Mexican label Otono. I told him about both projects: the rhythmically driven EP inspired by Esmeraldas and this second collection of ambient pieces. He immediately suggested combining them into a single release, with one side dedicated to the Afro-Ecuadorian, percussion-based material and the other exploring the more ambient, electroacoustic side. I thought it made perfect sense because the contrast between the two approaches actually revealed that they belonged to the same creative process. So, in the end, dividing the project into two complementary releases wasn’t my original idea—it was Luis’s. As soon as he suggested it, though, I realised it was exactly the right way to present the music. The Cayápas River and the Telembí community occupy a central place in both albums, but they never appear as mere backdrops or soundscapes. They become spaces of memory, ritual, and imagination. During your time there, was there any sound, encounter, or experience that decisively changed the course of the project? Everything was new to me. Even getting there felt like part of the experience. You can’t reach the community by road—you have to travel for almost three hours by boat before disappearing into the jungle. Once you’re there, there’s no phone signal. They have generators, but electricity isn’t available all the time, so you’re completely disconnected. At the same time, the place is incredibly abundant. Fruit trees are everywhere. You walk around, pick a banana, a mango or some cacao straight from the trees, go down to the river and start fishing. There’s a real sense of living alongside nature. But it’s also an extremely poor community. That’s the contradiction. Everything is beautiful, yet people have very limited access to basic services because they’re so remote. The government has largely forgotten them. What really struck me was meeting the local marimba maker. He’s a remarkable luthier whose instruments are highly sought after by musicians from outside the community. He harvests all the wood himself and builds every instrument by hand, yet he receives almost no recognition or support. Seeing that made me realise there was a political dimension to what I was experiencing. I felt incredibly fortunate to be there and to learn from them, and I also felt a responsibility to tell people how they live, what their music sounds like and what that community means—from my own perspective, of course. What impressed me most wasn’t just the landscape but the people themselves. In many ways they’re incredibly rich without necessarily thinking of themselves that way. They live surrounded by fruit, by the river, by music. People are constantly singing or playing drums, and music is woven into everyday life. They also have an extraordinary number of musical traditions connected to different moments of community life. During funerals, for example, women perform beautiful vocal chants that I would love to record one day. Unfortunately, when I visited there weren’t any ceremonies taking place, so I couldn’t document them. There are other celebrations where musicians travel along the river at night in boats, playing marimba and drums as they move through the water. They also have ceremonies where people dress in costumes made from leaves, preserving traditions that clearly trace back to their African heritage. What amazed me was that all of this exists just a few hours from where I live, yet most people in Ecuador know very little about it. That became one of my motivations for the project: to learn as much as I could and to show that this small country contains an extraordinary diversity of cultures that deserve to be heard. The visit itself happened thanks to a friend of mine, DJ Mamba System. He had already been there several times because he bought a marimba from the local luthier, so he knew the community well. You can’t simply book a hotel or arrange a visit online. You need to know someone. Families welcome you into their homes, often without expecting anything in return. My friend invited me to come with him, introduced me to everyone, and that’s how the whole experience began. They were incredibly generous people, and we became friends very quickly. So this might be a bit of a silly question, but do they have their own language? They speak Spanish, but some words and expressions in their songs come from Yoruba, reflecting their African heritage. It isn’t a language they use in everyday conversation, but traces of it survive in the music. What’s really interesting is that they share the region with an Indigenous community. I can’t remember the name right now (CHACHIS), but they’ve lived alongside each other for generations. As a result, some people also speak the Indigenous language, and the two cultures have influenced one another over a very long period. The history behind that is fascinating. A slave ship was wrecked off the Ecuadorian coast, and many of the enslaved Africans managed to escape. They fled into the jungle, where they eventually encountered the Indigenous communities already living there. From that point on, they shared knowledge, traditions and ways of life. You can actually hear that history in the music. Some of the melodic patterns in Afro-Ecuadorian traditions closely resemble those found in Indigenous music, so there’s this beautiful cultural exchange embedded in the sound itself. Did they find it strange that an electronic musician had come all that way to learn from them? Not really. To be honest, I don’t even think of myself as a purely electronic musician. I also play guitar and work with acoustic instruments, so our conversations naturally revolved around their music rather than mine. I did play them some of my work. They thought it was nice, but they weren’t especially interested in the electronic aspect of it—and that’s completely understandable. They simply said, “That’s cool. Thanks for coming.” What mattered much more to them was sharing their own musical traditions. They have an extraordinary number of rhythms and musical practices that very few people know about, and they’re genuinely happy when someone wants to listen and help bring that music beyond the community. In the end, that became my role: not to introduce them to electronic music, but to help make their music heard by more people. The remix album feels more like a continuation of the original project than a complement. Artists like Kelman Duran, Omaar, Siete Catorce, and DNZA take the tracks into unexpected territories. What criteria did you use to choose the collaborators? Were you specifically looking for them to reinterpret the material from perspectives very different from your own? The idea for the remix album came quite naturally because the original release was very short—it was only a cassette with a handful of tracks. Luis from Otono and I started talking about ways of expanding the project, and one of us suggested asking friends to reinterpret the music. It immediately felt like the right thing to do. I contacted the people I’m closest to musically and asked whether they’d be interested in remixing the EP. Rather than assigning specific tracks, I sent them the whole release and let each artist choose the piece they felt most connected to. I wanted everyone to work from genuine enthusiasm rather than obligation. Luis approached it from the other side. He reached out to artists through his own network, particularly musicians from Mexico, and he has a really good instinct for matching artists with material. In the end, it became a true collaboration—half through my connections, half through his. We also wanted to bring together people who have shaped what Latin American electronic music has become over the last decade. Fortunately, many of them are friends. Kelman Duran, for example, is someone I’m very close to. He came to Ecuador a couple of years ago and since then we’ve been constantly exchanging music and ideas. Siete Catorce is another artist I’ve admired for a long time. I think we’ve been in touch for more than ten years. I still remember hearing his music for the first time and thinking, “Wow, this is Latin American electronic music.” He was one of the artists who really opened that door for me. Luis also invited artists I deeply respect, like Omaar, as well as VIAAN, who is originally from Mexico and is now based in Berlin. Everyone involved already had a very distinctive musical identity, which was exactly what we wanted. None of the remixes tries to imitate the original tracks. Each one takes the material somewhere completely different while remaining connected to the spirit of the project. I think that’s why the remix album works so well—it doesn’t feel like an appendix to the original release. Every artist brings their own personality to the music, and the reinterpretations genuinely surprised me. You described these albums as a “message of Latin American unity.” At a time when much of experimental electronic music continues to look towards Europe or North America, your work draws on Indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian traditions without turning them into folklore. What does this idea of ​​Latin American unity mean to you, both from a cultural and a musical point of view? That’s an interesting question because the idea actually came out of a political situation. Ecuador and Mexico went through a serious diplomatic crisis after our current president ordered the raid on the Mexican embassy in Quito. As a result, diplomatic relations were suspended. There is currently no Mexican embassy in Ecuador and no Ecuadorian embassy in Mexico. Luis, who runs Otono, is Mexican, and I’m Ecuadorian. We were watching all of this unfold while working together on these records. For us, the project became a way of saying that, despite what governments are doing, we’re still family. We’re making music together, exchanging ideas and building something collectively. That felt much more important than political divisions. At the same time, Latin America is going through a difficult moment. Across much of the continent, right-wing governments are cutting support for culture while aligning themselves politically with North America and Israel. Cultural funding is often the first thing to disappear, even when basic public services are already struggling. We wanted these records to carry a different message: that beyond politics we share histories, cultures and values that connect us across borders. Our societies are also becoming increasingly polarised. Everything seems reduced to left versus right, with very little room for dialogue. Music can remind us that there’s something else worth protecting. Every country has its own cultural identity, but those identities also speak to one another. That’s what I mean by Latin American unity. For centuries we’ve looked towards Europe or North America for artistic reference points. We absorbed ideas coming from elsewhere and adapted them to our own realities. Over the last fifteen or twenty years, though, something has begun to change. More and more artists are asking themselves: “Who are we? What stories belong to this place?” We live differently, we think differently and we experience the world differently. It’s time we started telling those stories ourselves instead of letting other people tell them for us. For me, that’s what finding a Latin American voice is really about. Finally, could you tell me a little about Ecuador’s experimental and electronic music scene? Outside Ecuador, very little is known about it. Ecuador actually has a much longer electronic music history than many people realise. The great pioneer is Mesías Maiguashca, who moved to Germany and worked with Karlheinz Stockhausen and many of the leading figures of European electronic music in the 1960s and ’70s. He’s someone every Ecuadorian working in experimental music looks up to. The problem is that it’s still very difficult to make a living from this kind of music in Ecuador. Most people simply don’t understand it. If you’re making ten-minute electroacoustic pieces full of strange sounds, they think you’re either wasting your time or completely crazy. There are only a handful of people making this kind of music. Artists like Quixosis, Joaquín Cornejo and a few others are doing really interesting work, but we’re talking about a very small community. Recently I’ve also seen some exciting initiatives around field recording. There are artists organising hikes into the mountains where participants record environmental sounds, then come back together to process the recordings and practise deep listening. I haven’t taken part myself, but I think it’s a wonderful idea because it encourages people to engage with the sonic environment in a completely different way. Most of this activity happens in Quito. I live in Ibarra, a small town about two or three hours away, and the local experimental scene is almost non-existent. There are maybe ten people interested in electroacoustic music here. Everyone else is listening to reggaeton and going out partying—which is completely fine—but it means experimental music remains very marginal. I actually came to this music through metal. I grew up listening to the darkest and heaviest metal I could find, especially black metal. Ambient black metal eventually led me towards electroacoustic music, and suddenly I realised there was this whole other way of thinking about sound. Once I discovered it, I couldn’t stop experimenting. What keeps me optimistic is that Ecuador is full of sounds that haven’t yet been explored. The musical traditions, the landscapes, the different cultures—there’s an almost infinite amount of material to work with. Experimental music here is still a very small field, but I think that’s exactly what makes it exciting. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: enabl.ed :: IDM(R)ot I (Clean Error)
items.excerpt: Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct ERR101: enabl.ed
items.body: Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct ERR101: enabl.ed – IDM(R)ot I by enabl.ed   Clean Error label operator James Batista, a longtime IDM aficionado, continues to expand upon his enabl.ed moniker, a project that has spent years pursuing entangled electronics, glitch manifestations, and melodic fibers through another chapter, IDM(R)ot I. Detailed as ROTCORE, “developed to observe what happens to experimental music after its methods become part of a shared vocabulary,” Batista works at a high level of sonic fracture, clean errors, and digital misalignment, assembling a collection that “studies rhythm, synthesis, sequencing, sampling, digital processing, melodic behavior, structural irregularity, and intentional error.” Surrounded by a familiar cast of sonic crafters we tend to gravitate towards—ie. Cephlon, Romanowitch, Suumhow, Vaag, exm, rRine, Foel, Yaporigami, ENV(itre), Dragon, among others—enabl.ed finds its footing in disjointed rhythmic structures, where fifteen tracks lurch, stutter, flutter, and settle between lullaby tones and sharply articulated beats. Opener “initiate.rot.heirloom” immediately establishes this elegantly fractured language, allowing clipped rhythms and tiny digital disturbances to sit alongside softer melodic gestures. Batista’s sonic voice develops with remarkable consistency, even when the machinery catches on a few speed bumps, from the minuscule electro-entanglement of “rot.protocol\_113” to the roughened, shuffled beauty of “Reverb of a dead catalog.” Clean Error Records announces ERR101: enabl.ed — IDM(R)ot I, the next release in the label’s catalog and the beginning of a project examining the changing state of IDM through its history, production language and technological inheritance. Glitch becomes less an effect than a structural instinct throughout the record. Ambient threads seep through “time-stretched memories,” where stretched-out fragments seem suspended just beyond recognition, while “There are ghosts in the sequencer” digs into micro-textural repetition, letting clicks, granular debris, and sequencing artifacts accumulate into their own strange atmosphere. Earlier IDM signifiers surface across “time-stretched memories,” “Machine Empathy,” and “Failed Futurism,” yet each track pushes those familiar forms through enough processing, interruption, and rhythmic skew to keep them unstable. Melodies appear, fracture, loop, and mutate rather than simply resolve. Closer “Every genre contains its own extinction” hints at an even more pronounced shift in enabl.ed’s signature. Orchestral strings emerge amid organic glitch scurries in the background, creating a grandiose bookend unlike Batista’s earlier sound sculptures. What begins as digital fragmentation gradually opens into something more melancholic and cinematic, occupying an intersection between soundtrack music and IDM while remaining distinctly interstellar, tactile, and absorbing. Perhaps this new ROTCORE strata marks Batista’s next transmission. Here, rot does not simply signify decay; it becomes a productive process, a way for sounds to break down, recombine, and regrow. In that sense, IDM(R)ot I treats glitch not as damage to be corrected, but as evidence of life inside the machine—an opening through which IDM can mutate, regenerate, and find another generation of forms to cultivate and explore. ┌───────────────────────┐ │ R O T C O R E │ │ ERROR > IMITATION │ │ MUTATION > MEMORY │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ░▒▓████▓▒░ //│\ /// ERROR \\ //// BLOOMING \\ GENRE_CORRUPTION : 87.2% RHYTHM DECOMPOSITION : 74.8% MELODIC STABILITY : 41.3% ARCHIVE DEPENDENCY : CRITICAL NOSTALGIA SATURATION : HIGH ERROR VIABILITY : ██████████ IDM(R)ot I is available on Clean Error. items.body: Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. “An act of ecological connection” Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape by Visible Light   Located on the slopes of the Sierra de Luquillo Mountains in northeastern Puerto Rico, El Yunque National Forest is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest system. At almost 29,000 acres, El Yunque is one of our smallest national forests, yet it is also one of the most biologically diverse. For example, El Yunque hosts 250 different species of trees—about as many as are found throughout all our other national forests combined. Among other rare species, El Yunque provides one of the last remaining habitats for the critically endangered Puerto Rican Parrot. It also houses 13 of the 16 known species of the coqui frogs that Puerto Ricans have adopted as a symbol for themselves and their island. Yet a 2018 biological study found that global warming has reduced El Yunque’s arthropod (insect) biomass 10- to 60-fold, which in turn has led to corresponding declines in the lizards, frogs, birds and other creatures that feed upon these insects. Stunningly beautiful yet profoundly vulnerable, El Yunque serves as both a magnetic tourist destination and the home of the Indigenous Taino peoples’ chief god Yucahn (Yokahn). In February 2025, Minneapolis-based duo Visible Light visited El Yunque. Stunned by what they saw and heard, Amy McNally (cellist) and Matthew Hiram (sound artist) recorded many hours’ worth of nocturnal soundscapes in the forest and then shaped their own musical compositions in response. As Matthew Hiram wrote on his Substack, “the music was created in collaboration with El Yunque, as an act of ecological connection.” To me the resulting four-movement album feels like one extended meditation or deep listening event; it becomes difficult to tell where the natural sounds end and those of the human musicians begin. The album sounds almost like an acoustic version of the forest bathing contemplative nature walks that Japanese practitioners have introduced to the world. Calling the listener to pause and reflect :: And when Visible Light says they collaborated with El Yunque to make this music, they really mean it. In addition to the human instruments of cello, Moog synthesizers, rosewood alto flutes, sidereal gongs, brass singing bowls, and more, the voices of crickets, coqui frogs, and many other animals sing out on the album. And so do the voices of the plants themselves, captured by sensitive electrodes fitted to the plants’ leaves that pick up tiny electrical vibrations that are sent by MIDI to be processed and complemented, as Hiram has done on his solo albums like 2024’s Yucca Music.  Sierra de Luquillo begins with “La Oscuridad” (“The Darkness”), a more than 17-minute composition that is the longest on the album. Nocturnal keynotes of insects and coqui frogs take center stage, warmed by subtle cello and synth textures, calling the listener to pause and reflect on the peaceful beauty of wild places like El Yunque, to let it lighten and expand our souls. Later in the track the cello melodies sound almost in a call and response progression with the nocturnal animal voices, reminding me a bit of jazz musician and philosopher David Rothenberg’s famous duets with humpback whales on Whale Music. The next track, “Música de las Plants,” foregrounds plant voices. It begins again with the nocturnal sounds of coquis and insects, but now they sound closer, as if the listener’s ear is right up against the plants from which they are calling. Cello and synth melodies emerge and evolve subtly, almost like clouds passing in the sky above the forest. Then we start to hear the resonant hums converted from the bioelectrical signals sparking through the leaves of the plants. Developing slowly, the music moves at the more deliberate pace of the forest, not the heedless speed of the human world. Singing bowls add an ethereal, shimmering, almost spiritual layer to the processed plant vibrations. And even with all this emphasis on plant voices, those of animals remain foregrounded throughout, highlighting their importance and agency. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere :: “La Tormenta” (“The Storm”) focuses on a very common event for this tropical forest: rainfall, which it receives more than 6 meters (20 feet) of annually. On this track rumbling thunder and steady rain accompany the voices of coqui frogs, crickets, and other insects. I appreciate the percussive detail of individual raindrops colliding with leaves that emerges. Tasteful use of gongs extends the listener’s consciousness wider and deeper into the forest, helping focus our attention on darker aspects of the soundscape and how they resonate with our own inner spiritual depths—storms also roar within us at times, sometimes terrifyingly so, yet as with the outer rains in El Yunque, our own inner storms ultimately purify and renew us. I love how the coquis’ froggy voices sound almost joyous during the rainfall, reminding me of how the Prophet Muhammad described frogs as praising Allah with their croaks and cries. “Medianoche” (“Midnight”) closes the album. Here the insect and frog voices sound quieter, and the human synths and cello take center stage. The instruments do a lovely job expressing some of the uncanny, liminal quality of the midpoint of the night, which also holds the seeds of the dawn—a juxtaposition the listener can experience clearly on this track. There’s also a bit of a wistful feel to the cello, starting to bid farewell to this lovely wild and sacred place where even the local Indigenous Taino peoples did not traditionally dare to dwell for long. Rosewood flutes seem to express a kind of voice I wish we heard more of in the field recordings: the abundant bird life of the neotropics, complementing the cello in a lively back and forth that sounds like a vocal exchange between actual frogs and birds. The resulting warm sounds interspersed with heavy silences reminds me of how real animals listen to each other and to us just as much as we do them. Creating a tranquil, meditative, and spirit-expanding atmosphere, “Medianoche” makes for a lovely ending to this album. In the end I think Sierra de Luqillo does a great job of encouraging deep listening that can in turn cultivate a feeling of ecological connection, ideally leading the listener to practices of care and preservation. The compositions feel specific to this Puerto Rican place, with keynotes of frogs and insects and rain. Yet they also help the listener hear the importance of the natural places we inhabit wherever we are through newly attuned, more attentive ears. I also appreciated that Visible Light did not try to produce an exact sonic replica of El Yunque, but rather focused on the aspects that impacted the musicians the most, just as a landscape painter can highlight aspects of a landscape that a straightforward photo cannot communicate as well. Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape is available on Bandcamp. Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape by Visible Light The post Visible Light :: Sierra de Luquillo: A Living Soundscape (Permaculture Media) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Untitled brings a form of fantasy music where society or environment is imagined in an advanced technological and scientific age exploring the universe, time, future tech, and humanity. The monstrous and crazy hypnotic repetitive sound is the art of the impossible, famously indistinguishable from magic, a way to test new ideas and take tomorrow. Everyone is here riding into the unknown Untitled by RGL   The sound of strange science fiction dreams and dramas creating whole universes of the mind, with mutant ambient guitars, synths and beats, Untitled showcases a wide-ranging sonic palette, such as abstract drones placed alongside rhythm-driven tracks, modern electronic music that explores deep philosophical and psychological themes, encouraging the constant listener to contemplate the kind of future that waits somewhere ahead. If we don’t innovate, something else will. Untitled brings a form of fantasy music where society or environment is imagined in an advanced technological and scientific age exploring the universe, time, future tech, and humanity. The monstrous and crazy hypnotic repetitive sound is the art of the impossible, famously indistinguishable from magic, a way to test new ideas and take tomorrow. Let’s get started. The opening track is “I” (2:45). I imagine a twisted clock with sparks flying, heavy echo, busy guitar clockwork and pulsing electronic splashes. We are heading out into the unknown, with no name. Traveling like this distorts time, the sunrise starts again, “II” (3:48). Once the beat starts the sense of motion pushes ahead. I see endless fields and the electronic drone, with visitors speeding over the rising haze of sunrise, endless flickering misty tall grass fields. We move on, into the swirling darkness. A hidden orchestra warms up slowly, one or two at a time, then more join in becoming a slow imperceptible development of the environment and atmosphere, “III” (4:44) is like a sun bath, just sit and enjoy. “IV” (6:28) has a mysterious opening, entering into a dark Funhouse, a nervous fast beat shadowed by drones and other strange things, with voices somewhere else, it is impossible to hear people talking, but there are clues. Perhaps now we are riding next to the engine, things start purring as if under the rhythm of the rails, feel the power, steady and sure. The forward motion starts again with “V” (5:23), a strange wet munching beat, bobbing in the void with others, we are not alone and they are hungry. There is also a flute, which fits in an odd twisting solo over the strange wet sloshy beat that chews along at a slow and dangerous pace. I see distant embers glowing at night :: “VI” (4:34) starts with the sound of wet rocks, or perhaps the surface of a large body of water when it is very quiet, I don’t know. Maybe I see distant embers glowing at night, an old campfire by a new lake, more new things come and go but the main thing is the pattern itself. There is a huge rainbow glow in the sky which dominates the imagination. Next, on “VII” (3:18), the call goes out. The darkness is thick. The drone of the searchlight as it reaches into the inky blackness covers the visiting Martian judges, who are mumbling quietly amongst themselves. For the final séance the beats pick up as we go along into the end of it all, “VIII” (5:04). Opening into a frosty sparkling shimmering sunrise, phantom drones sustain throughout. Soon a beat bangs into form, abruptly kicking and tapping, the rhythmic machine builds and builds. The force stays strong, the elements shift and fit into new forms, bringing a host of wanderers. Everyone is here riding into the unknown. RGL is a Tokyo-based producer known for his lo-fi house productions and analog-textured dance music, with releases on labels such as Diskotopia and Breaker Breaker. In 2025, he released his debut album, Touzan. He is a member of the producer collective COSMOPOLYPHONIC and co-hosts the radio program COOL RADIO with fellow collective member RLP. The result is a work that crystallizes RGL’s distinctive sensitivity to sound and texture. Untitled is available on ato.archives. items.album: Hana Stretton :: tiarn (Self Released / Lima Loma / PW Elverum & Sun)

items.body: Hana Stretton’s album tiarn is filled with the kind of hazy lo-fi arrangements that pull on the heart strings of sepia toned memories, fading Polaroid snapshots in sound of private moments and community life alike. It’s not crazy to learn that some old family camera footage is part of the inspiration behind these songs. A seduction to enter into, like sleep itself tiarn by Hana Stretton   Hana Stretton’s tiarn is an exercise in dream reverie and hypnagogic songcraft. It’s a twilight album set between the edge of waking and sleep, night and day. It’s soft cadences are like the allure of the ocean, a seduction to enter into, like sleep itself, it catches you unaware and before you know it, you are inside another world with its own rules, its own logic. The pieces for this, her sophomore effort, were crafted during a period of time while living quite alone near the Pacific Ocean on its Australian shores. It was her habit to go down to the water and swim in the blue of dusk. These azure dips overlapped with the winter whale migrations, and perhaps some of their songs seeped into her own mind and soul. Water keeps things in the flow and ideas for music swam into her during her ritualistic purifications in the icy salt water. On the walk back home the melodies would surface and she would record these as the evening progressed. It’s this naturalistic process that gives the album its striking yet elusive character. Ideas for songs, poems or stories can come in a flash and they can come strongly, but they slip away just as easily. Paying close attention to them by the constant humming, constant singing, constant courting of the songs that wish to emerge is no easy to task, but Stretton has managed to coax these pieces out of that creative borderland, where there is always the risk of them slipping away, and into this suite of recordings that have made them very much alive. Stretton was born in Canberra, Australia, between Sydney and Melbourne. Permaculture, that mighty gift of ecological philosophy given to world by David Holmgren and Bill Mollison was born in Tasmania. One of my favorite principles from permaculture is the idea to “use edges and value the marginal.” It’s on the margins where different kinds of ecological systems blend together. It’s in the margins where different kinds of musical genres blend together. Here those genres are ambient and folk music, creating an idiosyncratic lo-fi blend. Her inspiration, as noted before also came from the margins of ocean and land, and it’s this dreamy characteristic between waking and sleep I find so pervasive across these wonderful pieces.   Bits of environmental detritus permeate the arrangements which consist of strings, pipes, synth, what sometimes sounds like accordion, many things I cannot make out exactly because of the way they are mixed maximalizes a sense of immateriality. Whiffs of field recordings, captured conversation, rain or wind throughout. The art of field recording reverses itself :: Field recording is now a folk art. Not only in the sense that the great ballad preservers of the past such as John and Alan Lomax went out into the field with reel-to-reels to record folk songs, but now, when most anyone can record environmental sounds on the fly, field recordings of the ambience of everyday life. That’s when the art of field recording reverses itself once again from being something that had once been used to preserve vanishing ways of folk life to becoming a folk art in itself. Hana Stretton’s album tiarn is filled with the kind of hazy lo-fi arrangements that pull on the heart strings of sepia toned memories, fading Polaroid snapshots in sound of private moments and community life alike. It’s not crazy to learn that some old family camera footage is part of the inspiration behind these songs. Before she was born her family had lived in Japan in the ‘90s. A young family looks over valleys to the mountains beyond during the summer. Her parents had also bought a synthesizer they never used while in Tokyo. She started using that synth and it was a way to reconnect to the past. Some of the sounds from the camera footage also make up the field recordings that were used—the hushed conversations, the rain, the wind, insects buzzing. This is the place where family tapes and home movies form another kind of private documentary, a documentary now shared in all its vulnerability. “Yet I know these soundscapes and songs were composed even if it feels as if when I am listening, that I am just caught up inside of Stretton’s daydream. It’s not a bad daydream to be inside of, especially on a lazy afternoon” ~Justin Patrick Moore Isolationist piano tinkles meet lazily strummed, half strummed, barely strummed, guitars and other instruments that just seem to fall out of the speakers effortless. Yet I know these soundscapes and songs were composed even if it feels as if when I am listening, that I am just caught up inside of Stretton’s daydream. It’s not a bad daydream to be inside of, especially on a lazy afternoon. The group singing of the choir who collaborated with her on the song “As It Was Before This” is one of the points on the record where the tension between the individual and community is felt. The choir is reminiscent of heavenly realms and oceanic expanses. A sense of communion with powers outside the self is heard through these uplifting voices as they bridge material and non-physical realms. This feels like a very private album, very personal in its overall vision, aesthetic and design, yet I hear a longing for connection in these songs. Other players are here as well, other voices. Yet the mingle in with her own playing, her own compositions. The word tiarn means landholder. Stretton shows her ability on this record to be a songholder bridging the realms of ocean and land, dream and waking life, bringing back treasures from the deep to share with the world. tiarn was released independently in August, with vinyl editions through P.W. items.body: MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. A strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects Birdsong by MEGAFAUNA   MEGAFAUNA is a project based out of Hazelton, British Columbia, a small town in Northern BC’s Skeena Country, deep in a landscape of mountains, rivers, and boreal wilderness. Operating under the self-described tag “despairtronica,” the project has built a catalog of IDM-influenced and breakcore-adjacent electronic music characterized by hard drums, fast tempos, and dense sonic construction. A September release is on the horizon that will return to that territory. Birdsong is something else entirely, and that contrast is part of what makes it worth paying attention to. The field recording and bioacoustics tradition has a long and serious history. Bernie Krause—one of the foremost soundscape ecologists alive, has spent over fifty years recording natural soundscapes and coined the term “soundscape ecology,” documenting how the sonic layers of an environment (biophony, geophony, anthrophony) create a complete acoustic picture of a habitat’s health. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology‘s Macaulay Library holds over 175,000 audio recordings of wildlife going back to 1929, including the world’s oldest known wildlife sound recordings. Ornithological vocalization analysis—the study of bird calls for species identification, territorial behavior, and mating patterns, is a genuine scientific discipline. What MEGAFAUNA does here isn’t science. But it borrows from the same raw material and pushes it somewhere considerably darker. Birdsong was commissioned by circumstance, an invitation to perform at the Midsummer Music Festival in Smithers, British Columbia, with a specific request for something more ethereal than the prior year’s set. The response was a 42:42 improvised piece built entirely from bird call samples, performed live on July 4th, 2026, with rain and thunder added afterward to reflect what was literally happening before, during, and after the performance in real life. The track listing credits specific birds by role—percussion (Shoebill, Crested Caracara, Lyrebird), vox (Quail, Three Wattled Bellbird, Bearded Bellbird, Capuchin, Horned Screamer, Screaming Piha), ambience (Common Loon, Helmeted Hornbill, Pheasant Coucal, Tawny Frogmouth), melody (Raven, Australian Bustard, American Bittern, Common Starling, Magpie), and keyboard (Crow). Whether this is satire, creative taxonomy, or a genuine documentation of sources used, it’s a uniquely compelling framing device that makes the listener hear the piece differently, starting to identify what each bird might be contributing to the overall texture. What MEGAFAUNA shows with “Birdsong” is a strength in honest field recording work and a meticulous approach to effects, how carefully FX are applied to these recordings and how that compositional process produces something genuinely interesting. None of it is repetitive. These are natural sounds being manipulated very carefully with dark ambience throughout. None of the atmosphere on this release is pleasant, it presents itself as a dark record, which is also what makes it strangely unique. When you think of birds, darkness isn’t the first association, unless you’re thinking of vultures or birds of prey. But MEGAFAUNA pulls darkness out of unexpected sources. The Horned Screamer and Screaming Piha are doing exactly what their names suggest, and pitched down and ring modulated, they become something else entirely. The first two minutes present something resembling a rainforest, birds layering and overlapping in what sounds like natural habitat. Then around the 3:30 mark, things shift. The atmosphere darkens and stays dark, little bursts of FX being applied to various bird calls, distortions and pitching manipulations building until the 23-minute mark where something changes audibly. A pitch-bending melody arrives like an echoing alarm, a new segment of birds being introduced, the composition pivoting into its second movement. At the 27:40 mark, another sound surfaces that reads initially as an alarm but is clearly a bird call being manipulated—low pitched, ring modulated, buried under heavy reverb, looping in a way that creates something deeply unsettling and hard to source. It’s the kind of sound that makes you question what you’re hearing. The FX work is what really stands out, the ability to keep ears engaged with bird calls and sounds for 42 minutes without the piece becoming monotonous is a genuine compositional achievement. MEGAFAUNA creates a dark atmosphere using nature sounds and electro-acoustic manipulation to take the mind somewhere it didn’t expect to go. Listening to this at early morning hours, at normal volume, lying down, not fully awake, is a specific and disorienting experience. It’s quite amazing for what it is: a live improvisation built from birds that manages to sound like a horror score composed by the landscape itself. Birdsong is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Lead singer Matt Hoy was raised by a single mother, and “Queen”, the title track of Birmingham reggae collective House Of Fyah‘s new EP, grew from what that taught him: “how powerful and empowering women can truly be“. The song salutes mothers, daughters and partners, down to the girls who will grow into tomorrow’s queens. His co-writer, keyboard player Tony Mullings, is a father of six daughters and has said he only wishes his mother were alive to feel it. Over Steve Clarke‘s drums and Mullings’ keys, Hoy leads an uplifting roots reggae anthem shaded with soul, which Clarke mixed and mastered with Dennis Jarrett. Hoy spent more than twelve years recording and touring with Ali Campbell‘s UB40, and Mullings, who grew up in gospel bands and spent years in the Bob Marley tribute band Buffalo Soulijah, has also played keyboards with UB40. Clarke, born and raised in Birmingham, opened Goldmind Studios in the 1990s, produced records for Sean Paul, Vybz Kartel and Beenie Man, and now drums for and directs Musical Youth. Jarrett toured Europe and North Africa with Sugar Minott, played with Black Slate and recorded with Maxi Priest. The EP Queen came out on Goldmind Records on 31 July, with “Queen” leading into the break-up song “Gone” and a cover of The Isley Brothers‘ “For The Love Of You”. In October the band spend a week in Jamaica for a live show, radio interviews and a video shoot tied to new material they are keeping under wraps. You can stream “Queen” and the rest of the EP HERE The post Daily Discovery: House Of Fyah – Queen appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by greenpete — This solo live acoustic performance by Jansch occurred during one of his non-Pentangle creative peaks. A 1974 show before an enthusiastic but respectful audience in Glasgow, it is everything Jansch lovers could want: just the man and his acoustic guitar. Many of the songs are from one of his best solo releases, L.A. Turnaround (sympathetically produced by ex-Monkee Mike Nesmith). However, absent is Red Rhodes' arguably intrusive pedal steel guitar, which on Turnaround gave Bert's songs a faux-country feel.. Here, one can better get absorbed into Jansch's complex fingerpicking. But he also mixes up the picking with some melodic but powerful chord strumming, notably on the autobiographical song "When I Get Home," inspired by a beloved uncle of Jansch's. Similarly autobiographical is "Build Another Band," about Jansch's attempts to find sympathetic co-musicians. Other highlights are the Pentangle song "I've Got a Feeling" (melody borrowed from Miles Davis's "All Blues"), "One for Jo," the progressive folk-guitar mainstay "Angi," "Fresh as a Sweet Sunday Morning," and Jansch's gorgeous re-structuring of a classic Christmas carol, "In the Bleak Midwinter." On the latter song he good-naturedly scolds the crowd for not recognizing the title after he announces it. And that's another bonus with this concert: we get to hear a supremely confident Jansch converse between songs. He even delivers a cool potted history of the song, "Stone Monkey."Thus far this great concert is only available in CD form. But we can be grateful the sound quality is superb. NOTE: the PA track listing for song number 13 is wrong on two counts. "Running From Home" is a totally different song from "Strollin' Down the Highway," both of which are Jansch originals; AND it's the wrong song! (Number 13 is actually a cover of the blues song, "Key to the Highway.") Still, The River Sessions, though as far from Prog as one can get, is essential listening for fans of this legendary musician.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Deep Purple releases a stunning 24th album."Arrogant Boy" features a classic Purple-esque sound, with Simon and Don guiding each other through a galloping melody; gone are the tracks of yesteryear?make way for a fun song featuring a Hammond organ that channels Jon Lord, Ian's tight drumming, and angelic vocals. It's high-energy vintage rock in the vein of "Highway Star," telling the tale of an angry Billy. "Diablo" brings a groovy, retro vibe with swirling, mischievous energy. A symphony of organ and guitar ensues, with Keith Urban treating us to a country-blues solo reminiscent of ZZ Top. "The Rider" feels a bit repetitive, with Simon strumming in a melodic heavy-blues style. "The Lunatic" is driven by the organ; its sophisticated, airy usage is surprising, shifting into heavy prog during the solo. "The Only Horse in Town" opens with a velvety, proggy keyboard part; it's a jaunty tune where Simon channels a guitar hero, transporting us back to the 80s. "Sacred Land" keeps the listener hooked, starting with a disarming, atmospheric prog intro. Thirty seconds of pure bliss are followed by a Zeppelin-esque riff, with a Scottish air adding to the journey."The Beating of Wings" offers a melting blues moment reminiscent of the band's heyday, complete with a nostalgic-style solo."Guilt Trippin'" is the radio-friendly track?4 minutes and 52 seconds of piano arpeggios and martial snare drums exploding into an incandescent scorcher. It depicts a dialogue between God and Darwin about where things went wrong on Earth; Ian delivers a unique, snarling vocal performance, narrating the story before giving way to two solos?one of which is a breathtaking honky-tonk piano piece. "Scriblin' Gib'rish" is classic hard rock: heavy, with sparkling keyboards and a blazing guitar riff. "Jessica's Bra" offers a spirited, moving, and fresh track, complete with a bluesy solo featuring heavy organ and frenetic piano. "Third Call" showcases organ work in the vein of Lord and Airey?you wish it would go on forever?featuring an apoplectic, exhilarating organ solo. "My New Movie" is a straightforward, flowing tune featuring a solo by Simon over Roger's bass and a keyboard break that makes you sit up and take notice; it's like a sonata?simply divine. "Splat!" reminds me of an 80s track; it serves as a finale for an eclectic electric keyboard solo?reminiscent of Stevie Wonder?with a distant echo of ZZ Top. It's a track that brings you back to life?a breathless 50-minute ride.Deep Purple stands as a prime example of rock's enduring longevity. Simon is the driving force; he forges an identity that doesn't merely imitate his predecessors, riding alongside Don?a knight-errant amplifying his musical excursions. The 70s may be gone, but this album is redolent of the memories we'll always carry with us.

items.body: AkA is a project founded by Frenchman Henri Sizaret. Now based in Portugal, AkA has a career spanning more than 30 years. This new release comprises nine tracks conceived as a form of litany. AkA’s musical world is fascinating yet difficult to pin down. Primarily an Electronic project, this album sits somewhere between Ambient and Experimental music, with various other influences surfacing from time to time. While the sound is at times minimalist, the compositions remain intelligent, with meticulous attention paid to every sound, effect, and field recording. Slow rhythms occasionally emerge, making the music more accessible. Vocals also feature prominently, delivered in various languages and a spoken format, or even whispered. This fits perfectly with the album’s atmosphere: mysterious and cold. A few tracks also incorporate female choral vocals, carefully sampled and blended into the background. AkA offers a unique experience, delivering visionary Electronic music, and “Echo Ex Voto” is a brilliant example of this. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Under Your Protection”: https://akamuzik.bandcamp.com/track/under-your-protection

items.excerpt: An acoustic guitar can make a room feel inhabited; on Dizzy Scent’s Doggy’s Cake, it also makes you wonder what else might be in there. items.body: An acoustic guitar can make a room feel inhabited; on Dizzy Scent’s Doggy’s Cake, it also makes you wonder what else might be in there. Fingers travel audibly across strings, gentle strumming takes on the unease of branches brushing a house after dark, and a voice slips between a confidential murmur and a disorienting chorus. Across these six songs, familiar folk gestures acquire strange proportions, with tenderness, sensuality, and distress sharing the same small space. Released on September 11, 2026, Doggy’s Cake follows July’s debut album, My Polarizing Nature, from independent singer, songwriter, and guitarist Dizzy Scent. She describes her approach as “dark raw,” pursuing instinctive playing and unusual chords while managing her career herself. In her account of the EP’s creation, depression, occult interests, and frustration with the music industry all feed into the work. Her attachment to imperfection comes with a pointed explanation: “Imperfection has a greater impact on humans because, with perfection, we already know what to expect.” That philosophy suits a record in which the movement of a hand across strings and an unguarded vocal sound carry so much feeling. The relationship between guitar and singer stays exposed, allowing changes in delivery to alter the character of an entire passage. The EP’s first track, “Witch (When Im Completely Red)” opens with acoustic strumming that scratches like the branches of a skeletal old tree against the side of a house at night. Over that dry contact, her soft, ghostly vocals develop a folky flutter, then climb into high notes resembling wind whistling around the building. There is something eerie and otherworldly about the way those two elements occupy the same space: the guitar feels close and physical, while the singing seems to drift beyond its reach. At nearly seven minutes, the opener gives that sensation ample time to develop. Dizzy’s release notes connect the song to her fascination with magic and admiration for Papus, placing its supernatural associations within her broader occult interests. The gently strummed opening of “My Dark Sides” has the plain, soothing shape of a lullaby. Her voice enters in a hushed whisper, suggesting an incantation murmured quietly enough to be mistaken for someone talking to herself. As the singing quivers and flutters, higher notes take on the character of a cry carried by the wind. The effect suggests glimpses of an inner world projected into the room, with the simplicity of the guitar making every vocal tremor more conspicuous. Dizzy describes the song as an effort to free herself from fears and the darker aspects of her character; the tentative intimacy of the performance gives those concerns a fragile, immediate presence. “Unchangeable” pushes the guitar forward with deep, resonant tones, its volume drawing attention to the sound of fingers gliding along the strings. Her singing carries a smoldering sensuality, almost jazzy in character, while retaining its folky appeal. A dreamy, ethereal quality surrounds that tactile opening. Halfway through, the arrangement becomes pleasingly unruly, resembling a chorus of ghostly voices, and her singing climbs higher while preserving its silky texture. The shortest song on the EP packs considerable movement into its two and a half minutes. According to Dizzy, it grew from months of searching for recognition and fielding opinions about her music before finding someone who acknowledged its value. She remains attached to the unusual chords and imperfections that make the work hers. Soft guitar strumming moves through “So That Means To Be An Artist And Sing ?” like footsteps on a moonlit walk. Dizzy’s languid, smoky delivery recalls PJ Harvey, its sensuality carried by the ease with which her voice drifts into the song. Around the one-minute mark, the arrangement and layered vocals become ghostly and disorienting for nearly a minute. A spoken turn and a grunt of pain follow that passage, before the folky singing returns and the sequence begins again. These changes give the performance an unstable emotional temperature, passing from languor through confusion to an abrupt expression of hurt. The title also echoes the question about being an artist raised in her accompanying statement, which criticizes the glamour and hypocrisy she associates with the music industry. More of the room is audible on “Blood Everywhere.” Ambient tone surrounds deliberate guitar strumming and a simple melody, while Dizzy’s vocals remain eerily hushed and murmured. Rattling sounds enter later, introducing small disturbances around the subdued performance. With so much space audible around the guitar and voice, those noises become unusually noticeable. The song’s unease rests in that exposed setting, where a quiet rattle can feel as consequential as a raised voice. A dog barks at the opening of “Life Is A Dog,” before gentle guitar strumming accompanies bluesy, folky singing. Her lamenting delivery carries a deep sorrow, with eerie layers of reverberant vocals gathering around it. Midway through, the song pauses for a spectral vocal passage, distorted and unstable like a voice breaking up on the radio or a cassette warbling as it plays. The interruption is chilling, briefly displacing the familiar intimacy of guitar and singer. When the earlier strumming and vocal style resume, that sorrow remains central. In her release notes, Dizzy links the song to anger toward the world and the suffering she has endured; the lament in her delivery gives those stated concerns an aching musical form. The EP takes its name from that closing song’s premise: life is a dog, and the cake is a piece of herself offered in response. Across the record, the guitar’s simplicity leaves room for a remarkably changeable voice, capable of moving from a folky murmur to bluesy complaint, sensual ease, or something suddenly strange and difficult to place. Her most unsettling passages grow from alterations to that intimate relationship, making the return of a familiar vocal tone feel newly significant. Dizzy makes her preference clear: “I love amateur art. It’s the most beautiful.” Her defense of instinctive expression runs alongside a wish to reach other people living with depression, a purpose she explains in the release statement. That desire for connection gives a generous dimension to her forceful insistence on doing things her own way: “Whether you believe in me or not, I don’t care. Because I believe in myself and my guitar. Fuck the rest.” Doggy’s Cake is out now digitally, with vinyl and CD editions available through ElasticStage. Order the EP here. items.body: A favorite from last year was Spirits of the Dead Are Watching, the debut of Believe, the Sydney-based quartet of Peter Farrar (saxophone), Novak Manojlovic (piano), Clayton Thomas (bass), and Laurence Pike (drums). Believe arrived as a mature working group, having largely negotiated their aesthetic off-tape. There's much care in their improvisations, which convey a particular reverence for the heightened space that opens when people play music together. All of the musicians doubled on small percussion instruments, and even when it got intense, the music had a ceremonial air, the band unafraid of rhythm and repetition, staying with fertile moments and drawing them out like silken filaments. That introduction was often a work of tension or calling-to-attention, and their follow-up, Nature's God —culled from the same 2023 recording sessions—feels more contemplative. It initially did not grab me in the same way, but I'm in its grip now. That first encounter was a victim of my own lack of care. Listening to Nature's God, one of the first things I noticed—or rather, one of the things that allowed much to escape notice during my initial distracted listen—is the sparse appearance of Farrar's saxophone. On the opening title track, he doesn't pick it up at all. The music develops from hushed notes with a sly and simmering urgency, Pike and Manojlovic goading each other along, the whole thing less a dramatic revelation than the dawning realization that the looming intensity of its namesake is always already present. Setting the saxophone down in favor of percussion reduces the instrumental contrast and further heightens the feeling of a collective sound, particularly in combination with Thomas's often percussive bass playing, striking the strings with mallets or its body with his hands. "Braided River" is a prayer, as beautiful and coherent a thing as free improvisation can produce, the saxophone arising and Thomas and Farrar so close in tone and intent that they're indeed braided into a new, quavering timbre. With the exception of the almost jazzy centerpiece "First Name Of A Flower" (which works itself into a fairly swinging groove by its midpoint), the pieces on Nature's God further underscore the ritualistic leanings that made Believe's debut so interesting. Small changes accrue but the music remains whole, like an undulating shape. Sometimes this takes the form of repetitive motifs or textures, as in Farrar's long tones and Manojlovic's delicate figures in the aforementioned "Braided River." At other times it is expressed in more explicit rhythm, such as the steadfast beat driving "Earth Does Not Need Us," the axis of a polyrhythmic swirl. Closing piece "Owls" is daybreak, that transition when the owls have settled and are handing the world back to the day dwellers. Again, no saxophone. The shimmering piano notes hang like dewdrops in a web, and every note, whatever the source, is allowed its full measure. At one point a flare of feedback breaks through, and for some reason I think of sunlight rising through dripping trees, of the moment a ray first strikes your eye and, although it is all so beautiful, you have to look away. Nature's God by Believe Also, check out the band in full flight on Clayton Thomas's YouTube page: Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
ENHYPEN have brought their THE SIN series to a cinematic close.

On 12 September, the K-pop group unveiled the music video for 'Checkmate', a B-side from their eighth mini album, THE SIN : BLISS. Released as a special gift for ENGENEs, the visual sees the members breaking free from their confines against the track's driving industrial beats and fast-paced techno rhythm.

The release concludes the narrative that began with THE SIN : VANISH and continued with THE SIN : BLISS. Built around the motif of “sin”, the series connects its music, lyrics, and multilingual narration as part of the group's larger storytelling.

THE SIN : BLISS also marked a new career high for ENHYPEN, earning the group their first number one on the Billboard 200. According to BELIFT LAB, the record sold over 2.09 million copies worldwide in its first week, becoming their fifth double million-selling album.

ENHYPEN will next take their ENHYPEN WORLD TOUR ‘BLOOD SAGA’ to Macau this October, followed by a four-dome tour across Japan from December through February and shows in Europe.

items.body: Friendship Survival Guide arrives as a blessing and a gift. In many ways we are still mourning the loss of Jóhann Jóhannsson, as his music is woven into the fabric of our lives. In the eight ensuing years, a few posthumous recordings have been released, along with a pair of box sets collecting his oeuvre; but the composer’s voice has been mostly silent since then. Enter close friend Adam Wiltzie, who earlier had collaborated with Jóhannsson on the scores for The Theory of Everything and Arrival. Wiltzie had held onto the analog tape loops from these sessions and later recorded guitars under the guidance of Steve Albini before Albini’s own passing, adding an extra layer of urgent melancholy. Friendship Survival Guide is an elegiac statement, approved by Jóhannsson’s family, that is not as much about surviving a friendship as it is about the experience of losing a friend. Wiltzie honors Jóhannsson while extending his legacy, completing an “artifact they created together” and offering it to the world in hopes that the healing might continue. As one might expect from the co-founder of Stars of the Lid, the music is as much ambient as modern composition, a melding of disciplines that forms a harmonious whole. The poignant “September Nineteen Sixty Nine” leads off the set; in this month, both composers were born but two days apart. The opening notes are like a lift-off, the launching of a life; in this case, two lives that would eventually intertwine. Immediately one is impressed by the brass and strings, the stately drama, the grand chords, surging first to one peak and then another. In less than three minutes, Wiltzie encapsulates all of his friend’s astonishing talents. The two-part “Dazed and Reflective Glory” introduces an abrasion of notes, like fading memories, corroded tapes, sheet music nibbled by moths. This abrasion fades in the second half as clearer, more insistent notes shine through, as if to suggest that time will not decorate this memory with rust. Every time the notes fade, we fear it will be the last, but we have learned otherwise. When the gentle choir begins to sing on “Mourners Will Be Outcast,” one thinks less of a funeral service than of an ascension, with new compositions wafting through the ether, descending through the clouds, borne on the mist and dew. Even as the choir recedes, the organ continues to play. Forboding clouds gather in “Exceptional Proportions,” threatening a deluge that thankfully does not occur. Instead there lies tenderness and hope in the nourishing rain of “Give Into Gravity.” The piece is an invitation to incorporate grief with its worthy companion, gratitude, and never to allow the first to walk alone. The choir returns like the acknowledgment of a prayer. The first single, “White Gloves & Turtlenecks,” is also the album’s shortest piece; and contains the album’s most overt violin melody, like a voice cutting through the fog. The track is matched with a video: the first part of a continuing story, promising more. In contrast, “Soft Favourites” is by far the album’s longest and most ambient piece, a soft reflection like a walk home from the chapel in slowly-falling snow. Midway through the piece, new chords emerge like visitations. The stars are twinkling, sending messages of their own. The title “In Ever Decreasing Circles” suggests fate closing in, the inevitable weight of time. Echo and breath populate the composition, along with some surprising glissandos that recall the score for Arrival. Yet this is only fitting, as a fine line exists between science and science fiction, just as there does between faith and fact. “Where You Are Now, Voyager” offers a clever play on words, referring not only to Voyager and its famed golden disc, but to the notes of a beloved composer, echoing through time; and to Jóhannsson himself, a voyager lost to us physically, but spiritually present, made all the more real through this exquisite resurrection of sound. (Richard Allen) Available here

Another ghost. Another shadow. Another thought. Another possibility. Another door. Another doorway behind the door. “Another” is a fitting word attached to a record that rarely stays where you expect it to. Cursed Frame is an album full of thresholds: sounds coming from across the room, voices emerging from the fog, something moving beneath the surface. Just when you think you have found your bearings, the music shifts the ground beneath you. There is always another layer, another shadow, another doorway behind the one you have just walked... items.album: The Low Culture Podcast: Betty Blue

items.body: Light percussion opens “Down Home”, the new single from Melbourne instrumental funk quartet Karate Boogaloo, before a bass line takes the lead at an easy mid-tempo. The drums lock into a hard, tight pocket on a kit that sounds close to falling apart, while organ and choppy guitar come in over the top. That rattling kit gives the rough edge to a tune named after anything simple and worn in. The main theme leans openly on nostalgia, and the band reckon anyone who has declared the riff dead should “check their specs“. Drummer Hudson Whitlock plays alongside Henry Jenkins on bass, Callum Riley on organ and Darvid Thor on guitar. The four met as classmates at a Melbourne high school and have played together for almost two decades. In our July interview with the band, Jenkins explained that Karate Boogaloo began strictly as a covers act devoted to The Meters and Booker T. & The MG’s. The change came with an original called “Stay Healthy”, which he described as the moment the band “crossed the River Rubicon“. “Down Home” precedes Access All Areas, due on 9 October through Colemine Records and College of Knowledge Records. In February 2027 Karate Boogaloo tour the UK, France and the Netherlands. The run opens on 3 February aboard V11, a 1951 British lightship docked in Rotterdam, and closes upstairs at Paradiso in Amsterdam on the 13th. The London date is at the Jazz Cafe on 5 February. Further nights follow at Hyde Park Book Club in Leeds, The Abbey in Manchester, The Jam Jar in Bristol, Le Tetris in Le Havre and POPUP! in Paris. Stream “Down Home” and order Access All Areas HERE   The post Daily Discovery: Karate Boogaloo – Down Home appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — By sheer perseverance and absolute luck , I landed on an online video of a piece from their previous debut album, recently released in September 2025. It was so good, I immediately purchased it on Bandcamp, as well as this November 2025 one. Why, may you ask? A multitude of conspirators united in getting me hooked on this new trouvaille, starting with the country of origin Poland, being an absolute well of incredible music in the past 40 years and still going strong. Secondly, my tastes have evolved very much into a definite zone of admiration for expressive bass guitar lines, faithfully adorned with terrific e-piano, organ and synths that come straight out of the instrumental jazz-rock, groove-fusion era of the late 60s and 70s (think Brian Auger, Booker T and the MGs and such) , all propulsed by a robustly-appointed beat factory. The energy is palpable, the passion overtly addictive and the mood positive and buoyant. If you are looking for depressive sonic compliance, listen away in another direction. The band is a trio (yup, no guitars) that favours a jumpy, organic, raw and yet plush style that could easily define the modern electro-jazz-disco-funk hybrid jam that one could enjoy with acts like Tobor Experiment, Bottazz!, London Underground, Project Gemini and surely many others yet to discover. Mind music one can dance to, tap fingers or feet uncontrollably and just smile along for the ride. Keyboardist extraordinaire Roman Wrobleski , bassist Orz and immaculate drummer Jacek Rezner combine to create real palpitating pieces that ooze class, sweat and brawn all in one groove.One can easily snap their fingers to the cool Pacific Coast luxuriance on "California Plum Color", a perfect introduction to their suave style, as described above, emitting a vintage vibe, not too far removed from those Ocean Eleven etc.. soundtracks. What makes this so compelling is the occasional twist in alterations, boldly inserting pools of effects and creative deflection to the highly melodic foundation. Roman's fingers dance over the ivories with skill and inspiration yet rigidly protecting the rhythm divine groove at all times.The similarly sized "Gradient 1" and "Gradient 2" for a one-two punch showcases the smoothness of tone and color, occasional swerves into hypnotic repetition that surely provides for bodily reactions to take place. Rezner's manic drumming sits well with the plump bass lines that cast the needed spell. The buzzing cymbal work in particular is noteworthy, a sizzling shuffle that swats indifference away like flies, urging, pushing and leaning on the pulse courageously throughout. The sparkling e-piano not only offers melody but also a high energy percussive slant that keeps the juices flowing, like layers of sonic terraces one after the other.The trio really keeps the pot boiling on the frothy "Antelope Color", the focus openly targeting the synthesized electronics as they become overtly experimental in the background, Rezner pounding hard and fast, Wroblewski whipping out a leaping organ rant and the bass keeping it all neat and orderly in between. Fascinating ! "Summer End Color" was leaving a hot and sweaty realm, gently blowing into a cooler expanse, as if frigid Arctic squalls intended to relieve the heat. The warm speed slowly winds down to a reverential ending.The highlight is revealed on the tow final pieces the "Oolong Color" clocking in at 4:39 and its extended 7:45 version, a dozen minutes of exuberant and expressive fusion of a substantial variety of stylistic categories that also includes ambient seagull screeches, a funk-jazz rhythmic palisade, and some grove-induces aural hallucinations, especially evident in the extended version, where there are some slight Ozric Tentacles sonorities (if one omits the psychedelic Ed Wynne guitar pirouettes) that keep the dreams alive. Orz and Rezner in particular revel in the electro-reggae shuffle, conjuring jungle fauna and flora images that feel like lotus leaves unfolding or giant mushrooms sprouting from the ground (artwork ideas for Roger Dean).Another precious discovery I intend to cherish, as I simply adore this kind of music.4.5 colour blinds

However (there's nearly always a "however", isn't there), I just can't get away from the fact (for me it's a fact) that this album sounds like a poor man's version of Transatlantic. I can't fault anything on the album - the music, the lyrics, the concept, the delivery and the production..... It's all very good. It's just that after playing cd 1 (sometimes I'll put on cd 2 first), I always reach for one of the Transatlantic albums (I have them all) in my vinyl collection. I just wonder, if Neal had condensed and confined this album to just one hour in length, would it have been a better and an easier listen. Yes, it would. So for me right now, just three stars.
